title: Your Agent Is Wasting Tokens and You Don't Know It - Erik Hanchett, AWS
talk_summary: A short AWS talk listing five token-cost controls for agents: prompt caching, difficulty-based model routing, offloading large tool results, capping tool loops, and trimming conversation history, plus observability of tool calls.

takeaways.what_they_do: Send the full system prompt once, then rely on provider prompt caching so subsequent calls send a much smaller cached prefix.
takeaways.evidence_quote: on every subsequent call, it will have a much reduced system prompt being sent over

takeaways.what_they_do: Use cheap models for simple work and frontier models only for difficult tasks; optionally let a cheap model choose the route.
takeaways.evidence_quote: don't use the most expensive model for everything you're doing

takeaways.what_they_do: Store large tool outputs locally or in cloud storage and pass a summary/reference instead of re-injecting the full result every loop.
takeaways.evidence_quote: store it locally or in the cloud and then use some kind of summarization that saves on tokens

takeaways.what_they_do: Set a maximum number of tool-call iterations so an agent cannot loop repeatedly or infinitely.
takeaways.evidence_quote: always set a max iterations of how many times it will loop

takeaways.what_they_do: Before deployment, inspect per-tool call counts, durations, and loop counts to find inefficient tool usage.
takeaways.evidence_quote: run some observability tools and take a look at the tool call use for every single tool

takeaways.what_they_do: Send only the last N messages and summarize older history into the context instead of resending the full conversation every turn.
takeaways.evidence_quote: looks back at the last 10 messages and only sends those back
